title: Adolf Hitler
summary: Austrian-born dictator of Nazi Germany from 1933 to 1945 who established a totalitarian one-party regime, initiated World War II in Europe by invading Poland, and orchestrated the Holocaust, the systematic genocide of six million European Jews.
card: Born in Austria in 1889, Adolf Hitler rose to leadership of the Nazi Party in Munich during the early Weimar Republic and attempted to seize power in the 1923 Beer Hall Putsch before adopting an electoral strategy. Appointed German Chancellor in January 1933, he dismantled democratic institutions to establish an absolute dictatorship, launched aggressive territorial expansion that precipitated World War II in 1939, and directed the systematic murder of six million Jews and millions of other targeted groups. As Soviet troops converged on central Berlin in late April 1945, Hitler committed suicide in his underground bunker alongside his newly married wife Eva Braun.
what:
Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in the Austrian border town of Braunau am Inn. After an impoverished youth in Vienna between 1908 and 1913, where he absorbed extreme antisemitism and pan-German nationalism, he moved to Munich and served as an infantry dispatch runner in the Bavarian army during World War I. Embittered by Germany's 1918 defeat, Hitler joined the German Workers' Party in Munich in September 1919, transformed it into the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), and became its undisputed leader in 1921. Following the failed Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923, he served one year of detention in Landsberg prison, where he dictated his ideological manifesto, Mein Kampf, setting out doctrines of racial supremacy, antisemitic eliminationism, and eastern territorial expansion (Lebensraum).

Capitalizing on economic devastation during the Great Depression, the Nazi Party became Germany's largest parliamentary faction, capturing 37.3% of the vote in July 1932. Conservative elites persuaded President Paul von Hindenburg to appoint Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Through the Reichstag fire decree and the Enabling Act of March 1933, Hitler dismantled the Weimar Republic, banned opposition parties, crushed independent trade unions, and established a totalitarian police state. After Hindenburg's death in August 1934, Hitler abolished the presidency, merged its powers with the chancellorship, and assumed the title of Führer, requiring military personnel to swear an oath of personal loyalty to him.

Hitler's regime remilitarized the Rhineland, annexed Austria and the Sudetenland, and triggered World War II in Europe by invading Poland on 1 September 1939. Under wartime cover, his regime organized the Holocaust, the state-sponsored industrial genocide that murdered six million Jewish people alongside Romani, disabled persons, Soviet prisoners, and other targeted groups. Historians debate whether this genocide stemmed primarily from a long-standing intentional blueprint or from structural administrative rivalry and cumulative radicalization within the Nazi state. Confronted with total military catastrophe as Soviet forces entered central Berlin, Hitler dictated his political testament and committed suicide by gunshot in the Führerbunker on 30 April 1945.

uncertainty.note: Exact dates of birth (20 April 1889) and death by suicide (30 April 1945) are established by official civil, military, and archival records.

how: Hitler's accumulation and exercise of dictatorial authority developed through distinct stages. (1) Post-World War I crisis in Bavaria allowed Hitler to leverage oratorical charisma, paramilitary street intimidation via the SA, and grievance propaganda, though the violent putsch of November 1923 failed against state security forces. (2) Reorganizing the NSDAP as a legal electoral party, Hitler exploited the mass unemployment and political paralysis of the Great Depression, capturing 37.3% of the Reichstag vote in July 1932. (3) Conservative political elites led by Franz von Papen maneuvered to appoint Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933, mistakenly assuming they could domesticate him. (4) Exploiting the February 1933 Reichstag fire, the regime suspended basic constitutional rights, enacted the Enabling Act on 23 March 1933, and suppressed all rival political organizations. (5) In June 1934, Hitler eliminated rival SA leadership in the Röhm purge, securing the loyalty of the armed forces, which swore a personal oath of unconditional allegiance to him following Hindenburg's death. (6) In wartime, Hitler directed grand strategic operations and authorized systematic ideological extermination programs, ultimately collapsing when Allied armies overran Germany in 1945.
why_it_matters: Hitler's dictatorship resulted in the devastation of Europe, the collapse of the German Reich, and the systematic murder of eleven to twelve million people in state-sponsored mass atrocity, including six million Jews in the Holocaust. The cataclysm of World War II claimed tens of millions of military and civilian lives, permanently altered the demographic and cultural landscape of Central and Eastern Europe, and precipitated the division of Germany and Europe into rival American and Soviet blocs during the Cold War. In international law, Nazi atrocities prompted the creation of the Nuremberg International Military Tribunal, codifying the concepts of crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity, which directly led to the 1948 United Nations Genocide Convention. Without Hitler's ideological obsession with Lebensraum and racial hierarchy, or had the conservative political establishment in January 1933 refused to install him as Chancellor, Weimar Germany might have weathered the economic crisis under an authoritarian presidential cabinet without embarking on continental war or industrial genocide. The legacy of Hitler's regime established universal benchmarks for warning against totalitarianism, state racism, and the catastrophic collapse of democratic institutions.

related.because: Hitler's aggressive expansionist foreign policy and invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 directly precipitated the outbreak of World War II in Europe.
Hitler's radical antisemitic ideology and state authorization directed the systematic industrial genocide of six million European Jews.
Germany's military defeat and subsequent economic crisis in World War I radicalized Hitler and created the political conditions for the rise of National Socialism.
The catastrophic devastation and atrocities of World War II under Nazi aggression spurred the Allied nations to draft the United Nations Charter to maintain international peace.
Widespread wartime atrocities and systemic abuse of civilians and prisoners by the Nazi regime compelled the international community to expand humanitarian law in the 1949 Geneva Conventions.

perspectives.holder: Intentionalist historiography (e.g. Klaus Hildebrand, Andreas Hillgruber, Eberhard Jäckel)
perspectives.account: Hitler operated as the absolute master of the Third Reich with a consistent, overarching ideological program formulated in the 1920s; territorial war and the physical extermination of the Jews were the planned implementation of his core racial blueprint.

perspectives.holder: Functionalist and Structuralist historiography (e.g. Martin Broszat, Hans Mommsen)
perspectives.account: The Third Reich was an administrative polycracy marked by structural chaos and institutional competition; Hitler often functioned as a hands-off arbiter, and policies radicalized cumulatively as competing party and state bureaucracies vied for supremacy.

perspectives.holder: Cumulative radicalization and charismatic synthesis (Ian Kershaw)
perspectives.account: Hitler's charismatic authority set broad ideological goals rather than detailed administrative plans; state officials and party agencies competed to work towards the Führer, proactively anticipating his wishes and driving systemic radicalization toward total war and genocide.
